title: Financial access is widespread but transaction and credit routes remain stratified
source_unit: FDIC 2023 National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households, conducted with the Census Bureau as a CPS supplement
geography: United States; nationally representative households, with state, MSA, regional, and demographic subgroup tables

observations.method: Biennial nationally representative FDIC/Census household survey; unbanked means no one in the household has a checking or savings account at a bank or credit union.
observations.uncertainty: The estimate is survey-based and household-level; it does not measure account quality, fees, geographic proximity, transaction success, or whether an account is safe and usable for a particular need.
observations.subgroup: All US households, with subgroup differences by income, education, race/ethnicity, disability, family type, age, and geography available in the survey tables.
observations.counterinterpretation: A bank account is a formal access indicator, not proof of liquidity, affordable credit, trust, or the ability to absorb a financial shock.

observations.period: 2023; banked, underbanked, and fully banked household classification
observations.method: FDIC classification: underbanked households have a bank account but used at least one of eight specified nonbank transaction or credit services in the prior 12 months; fully banked households did not use those specified services.
observations.uncertainty: The classification is definition-dependent and does not measure intensity, necessity, price, consumer satisfaction, or whether nonbank use complemented or substituted for bank services.
observations.subgroup: All US households, with underbanking differences reported by education, race/ethnicity, income, and other household characteristics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Nonbank use can be an intentional convenience, a remittance or payment need, or a response to unavailable or unaffordable mainstream services; the category alone cannot identify the mechanism.

denominator.unit: percent of US households; mainstream-credit classification frame

observations.method: FDIC household survey classification based on absence of a credit card, auto loan, or other credit product likely reflected on nationwide credit reports, plus reported use of specified nonbank alternatives.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not observe credit scores, approval attempts, pricing, delinquency, account balances, or the reasons a household did not hold mainstream credit.
observations.subgroup: Households by bank-account status and mainstream-credit access.
observations.counterinterpretation: No mainstream credit may reflect low demand, deliberate avoidance, recent entry, credit invisibility, or constrained access; it is not equivalent to bad credit or immediate hardship.

observations.period: 2023; technology, trust, and alternative transaction routes

denominator.unit: percent of US households; measure-specific question frames

bnpl_late_or_missed_payment.unit: one in eight BNPL-using households, approximate

observations.method: FDIC survey questions on nonbank online payment services, prepaid cards, buy-now-pay-later, payment performance, and reported main reasons for being unbanked.
observations.uncertainty: The measures have different question universes and do not establish whether technology expands choice, replaces a bank relationship, increases cost, or creates new risk for a given household.
observations.subgroup: Households by bank status, income, age, education, race/ethnicity, disability, and other characteristics reported in the survey.
observations.counterinterpretation: High online-payment adoption can coexist with banking access and convenience; trust concerns among unbanked households do not establish generalized institutional distrust or political action.

related_sources.claim: FDIC provides public-use files, code, data dictionaries, and multi-year comparison resources for the survey.
World Bank Global Findex supplies an international adult-level comparison, but its unit and questionnaire frame differ from FDIC household measures.
Federal Reserve SHED supplies a separate adult household-finance and credit-access frame.

boundary: FDIC adds a US household financial-access layer that distinguishes formal account ownership, underbanked use of specified nonbank services, mainstream-credit visibility, and digital/alternative transaction routes. It does not establish liquidity, affordability, remedy, trust change, consumer exit, or political behavior for the same households over time.
